intro: Revenue per visitor blends how many visitors buy and how much they spend into one number. Enter total revenue and total visitors to get the average dollar value of a visit.

sections.heading: How Revenue per Visitor is calculated
sections.body: Revenue per Visitor = Total Revenue ÷ Total Visitors — [the same total-revenue-over-total-visitors shape most e-commerce analytics platforms use](https://www.klipfolio.com/resources/kpi-examples/ecommerce/revenue-per-visitor). Every visitor counts in the denominator, whether they bought anything or not, which is what separates this from a metric computed only across the visitors who converted.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: $45,000 ÷ 30,000 = $1.50 per visitor on average — not what any single visitor spent, but what the traffic as a whole was worth per visit once every visitor, converting or not, is counted in the denominator.

sections.heading: How RPV relates to Conversion Rate and AOV
sections.body: Revenue per Visitor equals [Conversion Rate](/calculators/cr) × [Average Order Value](/calculators/aov) exactly when both are counting the same orders: Orders ÷ Visitors, times Revenue ÷ Orders, cancels down to Revenue ÷ Visitors. That condition doesn't always hold — if Conversion Rate is instead based on buyers, leads, or signups rather than completed orders, or if a single buyer can place more than one order in the period, the multiplication won't line up exactly with RPV. When it does hold, an RPV of $1.50 could come from a 3% conversion rate and a $50 AOV, or a 1.5% conversion rate and a $100 AOV — RPV alone can't tell you which. Checking conversion rate and AOV separately is what explains why RPV moved.

sections.heading: RPV vs. AOV vs. Conversion Rate
sections.body: All three divide revenue or conversions by a count, but the denominators answer different questions. RPV's denominator is every visitor, converting or not — it asks how much a visit was worth on average, blending traffic quality and monetization into one number. AOV's denominator is only completed orders — it asks how big a typical purchase is, saying nothing about how many visitors ever reached one. Conversion Rate's denominator is also every visitor, but its numerator counts conversions, not dollars — it asks what share of visitors bought anything at all, with no revenue in the answer. RPV is the only one of the three that captures both how many people buy and how much they spend in a single figure.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Assuming a drop in RPV means conversion rate fell. It could just as easily be AOV, or both moving in the same direction — RPV alone doesn't say which, so check conversion rate and AOV separately before diagnosing the cause.

Comparing RPV across traffic sources with very different intent without accounting for it. Paid search, organic, and email traffic can carry very different RPV for reasons that have nothing to do with the page or offer being tested.

Mixing visitor definitions between calculations. "Total visitors" needs an explicit, consistent definition — unique visitors, sessions, or another countable unit — used the same way every time; silently switching which one is meant changes RPV for reasons unrelated to actual performance.

Comparing RPV as a flat dollar figure across businesses with different price points. A $1.50 RPV means something very different for a $20 product than a $200 one; RPV is most useful tracked against your own trend over time.

faq.a: Revenue per Visitor (RPV) is the average revenue generated per visitor to a site, calculated as total revenue divided by total visitors. Unlike average order value, which only counts visitors who actually purchased, RPV's denominator includes every visitor — buyers and non-buyers alike — which makes it a blended measure of both how many people convert and how much they spend once they do. A $1.50 RPV means the traffic as a whole generated $1.50 per visit on average, not that any individual visitor spent that amount. It's commonly used to compare the overall monetization effectiveness of different traffic sources, pages, or time periods on a like-for-like basis.

faq.q: How do you calculate Revenue per Visitor?
faq.a: Divide total revenue by total visitors: RPV = Total Revenue ÷ Total Visitors. A site that generated $45,000 in revenue from 30,000 visitors has an RPV of $45,000 ÷ 30,000 = $1.50. Both numbers need to cover the same time period and the same traffic scope — revenue from a full month divided by visitors from only part of it produces a number that doesn't describe either period accurately. This calculator's own "total visitors" input doesn't require a particular definition, but "visitors" should stay consistently defined as a specific, explicit count — unique visitors, sessions, or another unit — every time it's calculated; switching that definition between calculations changes the ratio for reasons that have nothing to do with how the traffic actually performed.

faq.q: How is RPV related to conversion rate and AOV?
faq.a: RPV equals conversion rate multiplied by average order value exactly when conversion rate is counted as orders ÷ visitors and AOV is counted as revenue ÷ orders, over the same scope and period — conversions ÷ visitors, times revenue ÷ conversions, cancels down to revenue ÷ visitors, the same formula RPV uses directly. That condition matters: if conversion rate instead tracks buyers, leads, or signups, or if one buyer can place multiple orders, the multiplication won't line up exactly with RPV. When it does hold, RPV is a single number standing in for two different levers: how many visitors buy, and how much they spend when they do. Checking conversion rate and AOV separately is what explains why RPV moved, since RPV by itself doesn't distinguish between the two causes.

There's no universal good RPV — it depends heavily on price point, product category, and business model, all of which shift what a visit is worth before any performance question even enters the picture. A site selling a $20 product and a site selling a $2,000 product can both be performing well with wildly different RPV figures, simply because their AOV ceilings are different from the start. Rather than comparing against an outside number, RPV is most useful tracked against your own historical baseline, by traffic source or page, since that comparison holds price point and product mix constant and actually reflects whether monetization improved or declined.

faq.q: Should "visitors" mean unique visitors or sessions?
faq.a: It should be whichever definition is used consistently every time RPV is calculated — the formula itself doesn't require unique visitors specifically, but mixing definitions between calculations breaks comparability. A visitor who returns three times in a period generates three sessions but is still one unique visitor, so RPV computed against sessions will read lower than RPV computed against unique visitors for the exact same revenue, purely because the denominator counts differently. Most analytics platforms report both figures separately, so the practical fix is picking one definition, stating which one is being used, and keeping it fixed across every period being compared, rather than letting the denominator silently shift.

CORRECTION PASS (production audit): (1) Conditioned the RPV = CR x AOV identity in the interpretation section and its matching FAQ - previously stated as unconditionally 'exactly,' now explicit that it only holds when CR's numerator is the same order count AOV uses (CR = Orders/Visitors, AOV = Revenue/Orders, same scope/period); if CR instead tracks buyers/leads/signups, or a buyer can place multiple orders, the identity doesn't hold exactly. (2) Fixed an internal contradiction on the visitors denominator: common-mistakes item 3 and the how-to-calculate FAQ previously asserted total visitors 'should mean unique visitors, not sessions or pageviews' as a requirement, contradicting the visitors-vs-sessions FAQ's own (correct) statement that 'the formula itself doesn't require unique visitors specifically.'
